title: Sun and Skin
objective: After this level you can explain how sunlight helps make vitamin D and how too much harms skin.
summary: Skin makes vitamin D from UVB in sunlight. Too much UV damages DNA and raises skin cancer risk; WHO advises protection at UV Index 3+, and the CDC advises SPF 15+ sunscreen.

cards.headline: The same sunshine helps build your bones and can burn your skin.
cards.body: The WHO calls small amounts of ultraviolet (UV) radiation essential to good health, because it leads to vitamin D. Too much does the opposite. The difference is the dose.

cards.headline: A vitamin your skin makes
cards.body: Your skin makes vitamin D when ultraviolet B (UVB) rays in sunlight reach it. Vitamin D helps control the calcium and phosphate that keep bones, teeth and muscles healthy; too little can lead to rickets in children. One catch: window glass blocks UVB. That sunny spot by the window warms you up, but it won't make any vitamin D.

cards.fact: In the UK, sunlight from October to early March can't make enough vitamin D.
cards.context: The NHS says skin there makes vitamin D from sunlight from about late March or early April to the end of September. For the darker months, UK government advice is that everyone consider a daily vitamin D supplement. Same sun, weaker deal.

cards.headline: Too much of a good thing
cards.body: The WHO lists DNA damage and sunburn as short-term effects of too much UV. Over the years, it raises the risk of skin cancer, cataracts in the eyes and early skin ageing, and sunburns in childhood raise skin cancer risk later in life. A tan isn't a badge of health either: the CDC calls any change in skin color after UV exposure, tan or burn, a sign of injury.

cards.headline: What the WHO and the CDC recommend
cards.body: The WHO recommends sun protection whenever the UV Index reaches 3 or above: shade, especially around midday, protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses and broad-spectrum sunscreen. The CDC's sunscreen advice is SPF 15 or higher, reapplied after 2 hours and after swimming, sweating or toweling off. And the WHO adds one warning: sunscreen isn't a ticket to stay out longer.

mascot.line: Shade, hat, sunglasses, sunscreen. Sunscreen is the last line, not the whole wall.
